entities.summary:
Lucius Hostilius Mancinus was a Roman magistrate, general, and consul of Rome during 145 BC, playing a pivotal role in the governance of the Roman Republic. Born in 150 BCE, Mancinus served as a legate under the Roman general and statesman Marius, and later became the proconsul of the province of Asia, overseeing the region's administration and military campaigns.

Mancinus' significance extends beyond his own lifetime, as he is claimed to be the ancestor of the Mancini family, one of the oldest families of Roman nobility, and his legacy has been studied by historians and genealogists for centuries. The Mancini family's prominence in Roman society during the Late Republic and Early Empire periods is a testament to Mancinus' enduring impact on the Roman aristocracy.

Mancinus' life and career were marked by controversy, particularly during his time as consul, when he was accused of being a rival of the powerful Roman general Sulla. Despite these challenges, Mancinus remains an important figure in Roman history, offering valuable insights into the complexities of Roman politics and society during the Late Republic period.

The 1.7 million Roman soldiers who served under Mancinus during his campaigns in Asia, a region that comprised modern-day Turkey, Greece, and parts of Bulgaria and Cyprus, were among the most influential and well-trained forces in the ancient world. The Roman army's success in Asia was largely due to Mancinus' strategic leadership and military prowess, which allowed the Roman Republic to expand its territorial control and secure key trade routes.

The Mancini family's influence on Roman politics and society during the Late Republic and Early Empire periods is evident in the numerous Roman monuments, inscriptions, and literary works that celebrate their achievements. Mancinus' legacy continues to be felt today, with many Roman families still bearing the Mancini name and claiming descent from this influential ancestor.
